questions.question: Define reaction rate and calculate the average rate, in mol·s⁻¹, for a reaction in which a flask on a balance loses 2,2 g of carbon dioxide (M = 44 g·mol⁻¹) in the first 50 s. Explain why the rate over the NEXT 50 s will be lower.
questions.expected_answer: Reaction rate is the change in the concentration or amount of reactants or products per unit time. Moles of CO₂ released: n = m ÷ M = 2,2 ÷ 44 = 0,05 mol. Average rate = Δn ÷ Δt = 0,05 ÷ 50 = 0,001 mol·s⁻¹ over the first 50 s. The rate over the next 50 s is lower because reactants are consumed as the reaction proceeds: the concentration of acid and the amount of exposed carbonate both decrease, so there are fewer reactant particles per unit volume and fewer collisions per second between them, and therefore fewer effective collisions per second. Reactions are fastest at the start when concentrations are highest, and the gradient of the mass-time or volume-time graph decreases continuously until it reaches zero when a reactant is used up.

questions.question: State the two requirements for an effective collision, and use collision theory to explain separately how (a) increasing concentration, (b) increasing surface area, and (c) increasing temperature each increase reaction rate — making clear which mechanism dominates in each case.
questions.expected_answer: An effective collision requires that particles collide with the correct orientation and with kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy — the minimum energy needed for the reaction to occur. (a) Concentration: more particles occupy the same volume, so particles collide more often; more collisions per second at the same success fraction means more effective collisions per second, and the rate increases roughly in proportion. (b) Surface area: only particles at a surface can be struck, so grinding a solid into powder exposes many more particles to collisions; the number of collisions per second between reactant particles increases and the rate rises, while the amounts — and therefore the extent — are unchanged. (c) Temperature: heating raises the average kinetic energy of the particles, so a much larger fraction of collisions now has energy exceeding the activation energy; collisions also become somewhat more frequent, but the dominant effect is the greatly increased fraction of effective collisions, which is why temperature is the most powerful rate factor.

questions.question: Sketch, in words, the molecular energy distribution curve at a fixed temperature, and describe precisely how the picture changes when (a) the temperature is raised, (b) the concentration is increased, and (c) a catalyst is added. In each case state the effect on reaction rate, and explain why a catalyst changes neither ΔH nor the final amount of product.
questions.expected_answer: The curve plots number of particles against kinetic energy: it rises from the origin to a hump around the average energy and falls away in a long tail at high energies. The activation energy is marked as a vertical line; only particles to the right of the line can collide effectively. (a) Raising temperature shifts the curve toward higher energies and flattens it, keeping the total area (number of particles) constant; the tail beyond the activation energy line grows substantially, so a much larger fraction of collisions is effective and the rate increases strongly. (b) Increasing concentration leaves the shape and position unchanged but makes the curve taller — more particles at every energy; the number (though not the fraction) of particles beyond the line increases, so collisions and rate increase. (c) A catalyst leaves the curve untouched but moves the activation energy line to the left, because it provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy; far more of the existing particles now exceed the (lower) threshold, so the rate increases. The catalyst is not consumed and does not change the energies of reactants or products, so ΔH — the difference between product and reactant energies — is unchanged, and since it creates no additional reactant particles, the final amount of product (the extent) is exactly the same; the reaction merely gets there sooner.
